p.SYNC-ALWAYS-ENDS-WITH-A-HUMAN-APPROVAL-S: Sync-from-Code always ends with a human approval step.

p.this-document-is-the-checklist-for-that-: This document is the checklist the human runs at that step.

item.PART-A-SPEC-DIFF: **A spec diff**, shown as a unified diff against the current spec file (not a rewritten file).

item.PART-AN-INTENT-STATEMENT: **An intent statement** — one sentence per logical change, naming *why* the code changed.

item.PART-A-REVISIT-TRIGGER: **A revisit trigger** — the condition under which the decision should be re-examined.

p.IF-ANY-OF-THE-THREE-IS-MISSING-THE-PROPO: If any of the three is missing, the proposal is incomplete.

p.ASK-THE-AGENT-TO-FILL-THE-GAP-BEFORE-APP: Ask the agent to fill the gap before approving.

p.DO-NOT-APPROVE-AN-INCOMPLETE-SYNC: Do not approve an incomplete sync: a missing reason or trigger today is a lost decision in six months.

p.READ-THE-INTENT-AGAINST-WHAT-YOU-REMEMBE: Read the intent sentence against what you remember doing.

p.CORRECT-A-MISMATCHED-INTENT-BEFORE-APPRO: If the agent wrote "changed to 600 s because users on VPN need more time" and you actually changed it because "300 s was arbitrary and 600 s felt safer", correct the intent before approving.

p.AN-INCORRECT-INTENT-IS-THE-MOST-DANGEROU: An incorrect intent is the single most dangerous thing a sync can land — it encodes a fiction that the future reader will trust.

p.ASK-WILL-THIS-REASON-STILL-BE-VALID-IN-A: Ask: will this reason still be valid in a year?

item.example-durable-profiling-spike: "Profiling showed a 30 % hot-path spike on this branch" ← yes.

item.example-non-durable-i-was-testing-someth: "I was testing something" ← no. Revert the code.

item.example-durable-library-api-change: "The library we use changed its public API in 0.9" ← yes, but cite the library and the version.

p.a-non-durable-reason-means-a-non-durable: A non-durable reason means the code change itself is probably non-durable.

p.WHEN-IT-BREAKS-IS-NOT-A-TRIGGER: "When it breaks" is not a trigger.

p.a-trigger-is-a-measurable-signal-lead: A trigger is a measurable signal:

item.example-trigger-latency-threshold: "When p99 network latency drops below 100 s, per mon/latency-p99" ← good.

item.example-trigger-cpu-threshold: "When CPU usage exceeds 80 % on the hot path" ← good.

item.example-trigger-later-or-at-some-point: "Later" / "at some point" / "when we refactor" ← bad. Rewrite.

p.NO-TRIGGER-MEANS-NO-AUDIT-PATH: No trigger means no audit path.

p.a-permanent-fact-with-a-provisional-labe: You are shipping a permanent fact with a provisional label.

check-scope.title: 4. Does the diff touch only the affected section?

p.A-SYNC-THAT-REACHES-BEYOND-THE-AFFECTED-: A sync that also reflows paragraphs, renames anchors, or reorders unrelated sections is out of scope.

p.REJECT-AND-ASK-FOR-A-NARROW-DIFF: Reject and ask for a narrow diff that changes only what the code change demands.

p.omnibus-spec-edits-make-history-unbisect: Omnibus spec edits are how history becomes unbisectable.

p.THE-SPEC-DIFF-NAMES-THE-AFFECTED-ANCHOR-: The spec diff should name the affected anchor (`{#verification.timeout}`) exactly.

p.AN-IMPLEMENTS-MARKER-MUST-MATCH-LETTER-F: If the code carries an `// Implements: spec://…` marker, the anchor in the marker must match letter-for-letter.

p.stale-markers-rot-spec-to-code-traceabil: Stale markers are how spec-to-code traceability rots silently.

check-surprise.title: 6. Is the scope of the code change what you expected?

p.SKIM-THE-ACTUAL-DIFF-NOT-JUST-THE-PROPOS: Before approving, skim the actual `git diff` — not just the sync proposal.

p.AN-UNEXPECTED-SECOND-FILE-IS-EITHER-HIDD: If the code touched a second file you did not expect, that second change is either (a) hidden in the proposal and the sync is incomplete, or (b) unrelated and should have been a separate change.

p.HANDLE-THE-SURPRISE-BEFORE-APPROVING-THE: Either way, handle the surprise before approving the sync.

approve.title: On approval

item.APPROVAL-STEP-COMMITS-WITH-CONVENTIONAL-: Commits with Conventional Commits format (`docs(spec)` type), a body that cites the code change driving the sync, and the `spec://…` URI of the affected anchor:

approve.fence:
docs(spec): sync timeout into PROP-003 §verification.timeout
Code changed TIMEOUT from 300 s to 600 s after VPN latency measurement (2026-03-05, 847 messages, 128 users). Spec now carries the value, the reason, and the revisit trigger. Cited by spec://oproto/PROP-003#verification.timeout.

item.APPROVAL-STEP-STOPS: Stops. Does not continue into unrelated follow-up work in the same run — a sync is its own atomic step.

item.REJECTION-PATH-KEEP-THE-CODE: **Reject the sync, keep the code.** The code change was right but the proposal's framing was wrong. Ask the agent to redraft with the correct intent. No revert.

item.REJECTION-PATH-REVERT-THE-CODE: **Reject the sync, revert the code.** The code change itself was the problem — the proposal surfaced it. Revert with `git revert` or `git checkout --`, and record the lesson in the WAL's Known Issues if it is worth carrying forward.

p.NEITHER-PATH-SILENTLY-ACCEPTS-A-BAD-SYNC: Neither path silently accepts a bad sync.

p.a-silently-accepted-bad-sync-makes-the-s: A silently accepted bad sync is how the spec becomes fiction.

p.SYNC-IS-THE-ONE-PROTOCOL-THAT-WRITES-SPE: Sync-from-Code is the one protocol in the project that writes a spec change *driven by code*.

p.EVERY-OTHER-SPEC-CHANGE-IS-HUMAN-INITIAT: Every other spec change is human-initiated from intent.

p.a-weaker-driver-demands-a-stronger-appro: Because the driver is weaker — reverse engineering of intent from a diff — the approval step has to be stronger.

p.six-checks-is-not-bureaucracy: Six checks is not bureaucracy; it is the reason this flow does not produce drift of its own.
